subject: MGMT160
title: Environment, Culture, Ethics, Social Responsibility and Sustainability

questions.stem: Describe the organisational environment.
options: All the forces that affect an organisation, inside it and outside it
Only the competitors and customers in the market
The building, equipment and technology the company owns and uses every day
The natural environment around the office, including climate, air and water quality
questions.why: The environment is inside (employees, culture, resources, structure) and outside (economy, competitors, laws, technology, social trends). See §3.1.

questions.stem: Identify an internal environment factor.
options: Culture and leadership — 'how we do things here'
The economy — growth, inflation and interest rates that change what customers spend
New laws and taxes that force companies to change their products and prices
Social trends — changing habits and values among the company's customers
questions.why: Internal factors are the ones the organisation mostly controls: people, culture, technology and resources, structure. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Identify the five external forces managers feel.
options: Economy; competitors and customers; laws and politics; technology; social trends
Employees; culture and leadership; resources; structure; technology
Planning; organising; leading; controlling; ethics and responsibility
People; planet; profit; law; community and charity
questions.why: The five external forces are signals to managers who read them early. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Describe stakeholders.
options: Groups affected by an organisation's decisions, or able to affect them
Only the people who own shares in the company and receive its dividends
Only the employees of the company
The government departments that regulate the business and collect its taxes
questions.why: Freeman (1984): stakeholders include customers, employees, investors, suppliers, government and community. Balancing them is the job. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's mature answer to 'profit first, or people and society first?'.
options: A false choice in the long run — the real question is the time horizon
Profit always comes first, because a company that does not pay its investors will not survive
People and society always come first, because profit is only a reward for serving them
Managers should never think about profit; that is the job of the owners and the investors
questions.why: Companies that mistreat employees and society eventually lose customers, talent and their licence to operate, which destroys shareholder value too. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Describe organisational culture.
options: The shared values, norms and behaviours that shape the workplace atmosphere
The company's logo, colours, uniforms and the design of its offices and shops
The country where the company is based and the national customs of its people
The rules written in the employee handbook and signed by every new recruit
questions.why: Culture is 'how things are done here' — values, unwritten norms, and behaviour. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Explain the warning the chapter gives about a strong culture.
options: A strong culture can turn blind and reject change exactly when change is needed
A strong culture always lowers performance
A strong culture is illegal in some countries because it discriminates against outsiders
A strong culture makes the best employees leave because it does not tolerate individuality
questions.why: Strong AND open beats strong alone; a culture too confident in 'our way' rejects needed change. See §3.4 and §3.5.

questions.stem: Identify the three questions used to read a culture.
options: What values exist? Formal or informal? Competitive or collaborative?
Who is the boss? How much is the pay? How many staff are there?
Is it legal? Is it fair? Who may be harmed? Would it pass in public?
People? Planet? Profit? Which of the three comes first here?
questions.why: Three questions, a visible clue for each, a reading for each. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four questions of the ethical framework in order.
options: Is it legal? Is it fair? Who may be harmed? The public test
Is it profitable? Is it fast? Is it easy? Is it secret?
Is it legal? Is it popular? Is it cheap? Is it new to the market?
Who decides? Who pays for it? Who benefits from it? Who needs to know?
questions.why: Legal is the floor; fair means the same outcome if roles were reversed; harm uses the stakeholder map; the public test asks if you would be comfortable if everyone knew. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Explain the phrase 'legal is the floor, not the goal'.
options: Obeying the law is the minimum; an action can be legal and still unethical
Anything that is legal is automatically ethical, so the lawyer's approval settles the question
Laws are the highest standard a manager can reach, so compliance is the goal of ethics
Managers should ignore the law and follow their own ethics whenever the two disagree
questions.why: Favouritism is often legal and still fails the fairness question — which proves legal ≠ ethical. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four levels of Carroll's pyramid from the base upward.
options: Be profitable → obey the law → act ethically → give back to community and environment
Give back to the community → act ethically → obey the law → be profitable
Obey the law → be profitable → give back to the community → act ethically
Act ethically → be popular with customers → be profitable → obey the law
questions.why: A bankrupt company helps nobody, so profit is the base; each level builds on the one below. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Identify the three lines of the triple bottom line.
options: People, planet, profit
Price, product, promotion
Plan, process, performance
Law, ethics, charity
questions.why: Elkington's triple bottom line: people (fair treatment), planet (energy, water, waste), profit (still essential). See §3.7.

questions.stem: Describe sustainability as the chapter defines it.
options: Meeting present needs without harming future generations
Spending a fixed share of each year's profits on charity and community projects
Using only recycled paper, low-energy lighting and electric vehicles in the business
Growing the company as fast as possible so that it can survive for future generations
questions.why: Sustainability is measured on people, planet and profit, and lives in small operational decisions. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Identify the chapter's greenwashing detector.
options: Is there a number and a date, and does it touch the core business?
Is the logo green, and does the website have pictures of forests and oceans?
Does the CEO give a speech about the environment at the annual general meeting?
Does the company have a gift shop that sells eco-friendly products to its visitors?
questions.why: Numbers and dates convince people, not green pictures; real sustainability touches the core business, not only the gift shop. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Explain why managing responsibly is described as 'more visible and faster' today.
options: Every customer carries a camera and an audience — one bad decision is public in minutes
Managers today have fewer tools than before, so their mistakes are harder to hide
Laws are weaker today than in the past, so companies are caught by the public instead
Customers no longer care about ethics, so companies must be faster to win them back
questions.why: Social-media accountability, ethics scandals and sustainability pressures make responsibility the job itself, not decoration. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Analyse Emirates' first annual loss in three decades in 2020. Determine the chapter's explanation.
options: The external environment changed — the managers did not suddenly become bad
The managers made poor decisions about routes and fleet size in the years before 2020
The internal culture collapsed once the airline stopped hiring and training new crew
The company stopped planning for the future
questions.why: Emirates' managers did not become bad; the environment changed, and adaptation later brought record profits. See the answer to question 2 in §3.1.

questions.stem: Classify the UAE tax on sugary drinks that made drink companies redesign products.
options: External force — laws and politics
Internal factor — culture and leadership
External force — social trends
Internal factor — technology and resources
questions.why: Taxes and regulations are the 'laws and politics' external force. See the table in §3.2.

questions.stem: Classify health awareness that pushed cafés to offer low-sugar menus.
options: External force — social trends
External force — technology
Internal factor — structure
External force — economy
questions.why: Changing habits and values are social trends; customers asked first. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Classify a late schedule change that floods the registrar with complaints and overloads staff.
options: An internal weakness felt everywhere
An external threat from competitors offering a better timetable
A social trend among students towards complaining online
An economic force that reduces the university's budget for staff
questions.why: One internal weakness spreads through the organisation — that is why managers check the inside first. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Analyse the hotel scan: high front-desk turnover, an outdated booking system, strong cash now, and two new hotels opening next year. Determine the best decision.
options: Fix the turnover and upgrade the booking system this year, while cash is strong and before competitors open
Wait until the new hotels open and then react to whatever prices and services they offer
Cut prices immediately so that the new hotels find it hard to win customers when they open
Close the front desk and move all bookings to an app, so that staff turnover no longer matters
questions.why: Connect an internal weakness to an external threat and act early. See the sample scan in §3.2.

questions.stem: Determine the stakeholder group that wants stable, fair partnerships.
options: Suppliers
Investors
Government
Customers
questions.why: Suppliers want stable, fair partnerships; investors want returns; government wants compliance and taxes; customers want quality and fair prices. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Determine the fitting culture for an airline's aircraft maintenance operation.
options: Traditional — formal rules, clear hierarchy, defined procedures
Google-style — freedom in how you work, open desks and room for improvisation
No fixed culture — each engineer decides the method that fits the aircraft in front of them
A sales-style competitive culture in which engineers compete on the number of aircraft serviced
questions.why: Where one improvisation can be a disaster, a careful, predictable culture fits. Neither culture is 'right' — each fits its situation. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a sports team where players compete hard for starting positions, yet substitutes celebrate goals they did not score. Determine the reading.
options: Competition inside a collaborative frame — the healthiest mix
A purely competitive culture, because players are fighting each other for starting positions
A purely collaborative culture, because everyone celebrates together whoever scores
A culture with no clear values, because the players' behaviour contradicts itself
questions.why: Reading a culture: the clue (substitutes celebrate) shows collaboration framing the competition. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Determine the verdict on a manager who gives the best shifts to his friends.
options: Unethical — it fails the fairness question, even though it is usually legal
Ethical — managers may arrange the schedule as they see best
Ethical — it is legal, and legal is the standard by which a manager's actions are judged
It depends on the size of the company and whether the other staff have complained
questions.why: Favouritism fails Q2 (fair?) and is often legal — which proves legal ≠ ethical. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Determine the verdict on employee monitoring.
options: It depends — announced, proportionate, work-related monitoring passes; secret spying fails
Always ethical — the employer owns the equipment and pays for the employee's time
Always unethical — monitoring shows a lack of trust that destroys engagement
Ethical only for senior staff, whose decisions carry more risk for the company
questions.why: Secret spying fails the fairness and public tests — would you tell them? See §3.6.

questions.stem: Determine the verdict on an app that hides fees until checkout.
options: Unethical — built to pass unnoticed, which fails the fairness and public tests
Ethical — the customer can still cancel at checkout once the full price is shown
Ethical — all apps do it, and customers have come to expect fees at checkout
It depends on the size of the fee and whether it is mentioned somewhere in the terms
questions.why: Hiding fees fails Q2 and Q4; being built to pass unnoticed is the confession. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Analyse the product problem — a known fault, not dangerous today, costly to fix, invisible to most customers. Determine the chapter's position.
options: Fix it, announce it honestly and turn the fix into a trust story
Ignore it — most customers will never notice, and the fault is not dangerous today
Wait until customers complain and then fix each case individually at the company's cost
Fix it quietly in the next production run without telling anyone that a fault existed
questions.why: Ignoring may pass 'legal' and fails fair, harm and the public test; Volkswagen hid its diesel problem and paid tens of billions. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Determine the level of Carroll's pyramid for a company that gives to charity while cheating its customers.
options: It fails — charity cannot wash away cheating at the lower levels
The top level — giving back to the community is the highest responsibility a company can show
The ethical level — the company is doing more than the law requires by giving to charity
The legal level — the company is operating within the law and paying its taxes
questions.why: Each level builds on the one below; giving back does not cancel unethical behaviour. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Select the sustainability idea that is a genuine win–win for a university.
options: Smart classroom cooling schedules — less energy and a smaller bill
Painting the campus buildings green
A speech by the president about the planet at the start of each academic year
A sustainability poster in the gift shop next to the recycled-paper notebooks
questions.why: The best ideas name both wins — the planet effect and the money effect — and are decided by ordinary managers. See §3.7 and the take-away.

questions.stem: Compare two sustainability claims: 'We care deeply about the planet' and 'Cut packaging waste 30% by 2027'. Determine which passes the greenwashing test.
options: The second — it has a number and a date
The first — it shows real feeling
Both pass equally
Neither — companies cannot be sustainable
questions.why: Numbers and dates convince; adjectives do not. See the greenwashing detector in §3.7.

questions.stem: Identify the four internal environment factors.
options: People, culture and leadership, technology and resources, structure
Economy, competitors, laws and politics, technology
Customers, suppliers, investors and government
Profit, people, planet and the law
questions.why: Internal factors are the ones the organisation mostly controls. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Explain why managers check the inside of the organisation first.
options: One internal weakness spreads through the whole organisation
The outside environment never changes, so there is nothing to scan there
Internal factors cannot be controlled, so they must be identified before anything else
Customers do not matter until the organisation has sorted out its own problems
questions.why: An internal weakness is felt everywhere, so managers scan inside first. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Describe the 'economy' external force.
options: Growth, inflation and interest rates that change what customers can spend
The rules, regulations and taxes set by the government of the country
Changing habits and values in society that alter what customers want
New tools and software that change how products are made and delivered
questions.why: Economic forces change customers' spending power. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Describe the 'technology' external force.
options: New tools that change how products are made, sold and delivered
Taxes on sugary drinks that force companies to redesign their products
Health awareness among customers that pushes cafés to change their menus
A new competitor opening nearby
questions.why: Technology changes how work is done; managers who read it early win. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Explain what managers do with the five external forces.
options: Read them early as signals and adapt before competitors do
Ignore them, because they cannot be controlled
Wait until they become real problems and then respond with a detailed plan
Report them to the government so that it can protect the industry
questions.why: External forces are signals for managers who read them early. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Identify the stakeholder groups named in the chapter.
options: Customers, employees, investors, suppliers, government and community
Only the shareholders who own the company and receive its dividends
Only the customers who buy the products and the employees who make them
The managers and owners who make the decisions about the business
questions.why: Freeman (1984): stakeholders are all groups affected by, or able to affect, the organisation. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Explain what balancing stakeholders means.
options: Making decisions that serve several groups' needs over time, not one group only
Giving every stakeholder group the same amount of money each year
Always choosing the investors first, because they own the company
Letting the local community decide how the business should be run
questions.why: Balancing stakeholders is the manager's job. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Describe the difference between a strong culture and an open culture.
options: A strong culture has shared values everyone follows; an open culture also welcomes change and new ideas
Strong means a culture in a big company; open means a culture in a small start-up
They mean the same thing, and the chapter uses the two words interchangeably
An open culture has no shared values, so employees are free to behave as they like
questions.why: Strong AND open beats strong alone. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Explain the phrase 'how we do things here'.
options: It is the simplest definition of organisational culture
It is the company's mission statement, printed on the wall of the reception area
It is the employee handbook that every new recruit signs on the first day
It is the organisation chart showing who reports to whom in the company
questions.why: Culture = shared values, norms and behaviours — how things are done here. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Describe the visible clue for a formal culture.
options: Titles, dress codes, scheduled meetings and written procedures
First names, open desks and quick chats in the corridor instead of meetings
Substitutes celebrating goals they did not score from the bench
A green logo and pictures of forests on the company website
questions.why: Formal cultures show in titles, dress and procedures. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Describe the visible clue for a collaborative culture.
options: People share credit and help each other without being asked
People compete for the best shifts and the most interesting projects
Everyone works alone in silence
Managers decide everything and staff wait to be told what to do
questions.why: Collaboration shows in shared credit and unasked help. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Explain why reading a culture matters for a new manager.
options: It tells you how decisions really get made and what behaviour will be accepted
It shows the company's profit and how it compares with its competitors
It is required by law before a new manager can be appointed to the post
It replaces the need to plan, because the culture already decides what will happen
questions.why: Reading the culture is how you avoid breaking unwritten rules. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Describe the public test.
options: Ask whether you would be comfortable if everyone knew what you did
Ask whether the public will buy the product once it is launched
Ask the government for permission before taking the action
Ask whether the action is profitable enough to justify the risk
questions.why: Q4 of the framework: would you be comfortable if it were public. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Describe the fairness question.
options: Ask whether you would accept the same outcome if the roles were reversed
Ask whether the law allows the action in the country where you operate
Ask whether the action makes money for the company and its investors
Ask whether the boss agrees with the decision before you act on it
questions.why: Q2: fair means the same outcome if roles were reversed. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Explain why ethics scandals are more expensive today.
options: Every customer carries a camera and an audience, so one bad decision is public in minutes
Laws are stricter than ever and fines for ethical failures have risen sharply
Companies have less money than before, so they cannot afford to pay for scandals
Customers are angrier than before and boycott companies more readily
questions.why: Social-media accountability makes responsibility the job itself. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's conclusion about responsibility.
options: Managing responsibly is the job itself, not decoration added after profit
Responsibility is a marketing cost
Only large companies need to manage responsibly, because only they are watched
Responsibility belongs to the legal department, which checks every decision
questions.why: Responsibility is the job, not decoration. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Identify the three pressures the chapter says make responsibility visible and fast.
options: Social-media accountability, ethics scandals and sustainability pressure
Taxes, tariffs and rising interest rates
Hiring, firing and training employees
Planning, organising and controlling the work
questions.why: These three pressures shape responsible management today. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Classify a café whose best barista quit and whose coffee quality fell.
options: An internal factor — people
An external force — economy
An external force — social trends
An external force — laws
questions.why: People are an internal factor the organisation mostly controls. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Classify a hotel's old booking software that crashes at peak times.
options: An internal factor — technology and resources
An external force — technology changing how hotels are booked
An external force — competitors with better booking systems
A social trend towards booking hotels online at the last minute
questions.why: The hotel's own systems are internal. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who blames staff when a company loses money during a global recession. Determine the chapter's view.
options: The external environment changed; managers must adapt rather than blame
The staff caused the recession by demanding higher pay and working fewer hours
Blaming staff is good control
The company should close, because a recession makes profitable management impossible
questions.why: Emirates' 2020 loss shows the environment, not bad managers, caused the fall. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Select the stakeholder group that wants quality and fair prices.
options: Customers
Investors
Government
Suppliers
questions.why: Customers want quality at fair prices. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a company that pays record dividends by cutting staff pay below the market. Determine the long-run risk.
options: Losing talent and reputation, which eventually destroys shareholder value too
No risk — investors come first, and employees can always find work elsewhere
Customers will pay more for the products because the company is clearly well run
The government will reward the company for its strong financial performance
questions.why: Mistreating one stakeholder group costs the others later. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Determine the stakeholder group that wants compliance and taxes.
options: Government
Community
Employees
Customers
questions.why: Government wants compliance and taxes. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Select the fitting culture for a game-design studio inventing new products.
options: An open, flexible culture with freedom in how you work
A traditional culture with strict procedures and a clear chain of command
A culture with no values at all, so that nothing limits the designers' imagination
A military-style hierarchy in which every design decision is approved from the top
questions.why: Creative work needs freedom; a careful culture fits safety-critical work. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a company with a very strong culture that rejected a needed change. Determine the chapter's warning.
options: A strong culture can turn blind — strong and open beats strong alone
Strong cultures always succeed in the end because employees are committed to them
Weak cultures are better because they offer no resistance to change
Culture does not affect change; only the budget and the timetable matter
questions.why: Strong AND open. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Determine the culture signal when new ideas are met with 'we have always done it this way'.
options: A strong but closed culture
An open culture that has learned from experience
A collaborative culture in which everyone agrees
No culture at all, because nobody has thought about the question
questions.why: Rejecting change is the sign of a closed culture. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Classify a workplace where everyone uses first names, sits at open desks and decides in quick chats.
options: Informal
Formal
Competitive
Closed
questions.why: First names and quick chats are informal clues. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Classify a sales floor where staff hide leads from each other.
options: Competitive without a collaborative frame
Collaborative, because staff are protecting the team's results
Formal, because leads are recorded and tracked individually
Informal, because staff are managing their own leads without rules
questions.why: Hiding leads is pure competition, not competition inside collaboration. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Determine the first thing a new manager should do to read the culture.
options: Watch for the visible clues: how people dress, speak, decide and share credit
Rewrite the values poster so that it describes the culture the manager wants
Change the dress code to signal that a new manager has arrived
Ask the CEO for the profit figures and the latest organisation chart
questions.why: Three questions, a clue for each. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Classify a firm that obeys the law and makes profit but cheats no one and gives nothing back.
options: It reaches the ethical level but not the top level of Carroll's pyramid
It reaches the top level, because cheating nobody is the highest form of responsibility
It fails the legal level, because giving nothing back to the community is a legal duty
It fails the profit level, because a firm that gives nothing back cannot stay profitable
questions.why: Profitable, legal, ethical — giving back is the fourth level. See §3.7.
